but says it had little impact7h agoZia Yusuf says he does not agree with Suella Braverman's claim minority ethnic people can't be English8h agoMiliband acknowledges ‘difficult’ relations between US and Ukraine’s allies8h agoMiliband says Europe needs to revive debate on what it does with frozen Russian assets8h agoFarage denies Reform would let troops shoot small boats after Jenrick’s ‘lethal force’ claim8h agoSNP invites Burnham to its party conference, saying his defence of union has made constitution 'central question' in politics8h agoStandards watchdog warns Burnham of growing concern that wealthy donors exercising 'undue influence' on politics9h agoIMF raises UK growth forecast as economist says Healey should ‘stay the course’9h agoAndy Burnham will take Britain back into European Union, Neil Kinnock claims Ken McCallum Photograph: Danny Lawson/PAView image in fullscreenKen McCallum Photograph: Danny Lawson/PAAndrew SparrowTue 13 Oct 2026 17.23 BSTFirst published on Tue 13 Oct 2026 09.13 BSTShareFrom 5h ago13.15 BSTMI5 chief Ken McCallum confirms Russia did interfere in Brexit referendum - but says it had little impactDan SabbaghDan Sabbagh is the Guardian’s defence and security editor.

MI5 chief Ken McCallum said today that Moscow did attempt to interfere in the 2016 Brexit referendum with anti-EU coverage on RT and Sputnik media and via troll social media accounts. But there was a big difference between “what may have been attempted and what actually resulted”, he added.

The head of the Security Service said that he agreed strongly with what the prime minister had said on Sunday and Monday, when he raised the issue of attempted Russian interference a decade ago – though Burnham then backed off when he was challenged by the Conservatives as to whether this meant he regarded the Brexit vote as illegitimate.

McCallum did not put any new evidence into the public domain but cited already known concerns about Russian broadcasters who “came in pretty strongly around the time of the referendum” in favour of Brexit. He also said that “there was a second line of interference attempted through [internet] trolls”.

However, he argued there was no evidence to suggest the result of the Brexit vote had been swayed as a result of the effort, which is generally believed to have been marginal, and said that it would be to Russia’s benefit if the issue was talked about further.

double quotation markIt is up to us how far we allow our adversaries to divide us.

I’m a little bit worried that if we all stay in this debate for another few days, the Russian trolls who didn’t appear to do all that much at various points over the years, they’ll be delighted they are front page news once again despite the comparative unimpressedness of what they do at all points along the journey.

I am a little bit anxious that we don’t play into our adversaries’ hands by making these trolls look 10ft tall.

double quotation markThere is a really important difference between interference attempted and outcome swayed … It’s quite important to focus on the difference between what may have been attempted and what actually resulted.

It is a matter of public record including in select committee reports published in 2019 – the DCMS [digital, culture, media and sport] committee did a bit and the intelligence and security committee did a bit also – that in 2016, before you even get to any secret intelligence … it is openly on the record that Russia Today and Sputnik and other Russian media organisations came in pretty strongly around the referendum.

And it is also a matter of open source record that there was a certain amount of interference attempted through trolls and bots and so forth.

I agree strongly with what the prime minister said yesterday, we did see a hack and leak thing inside the 2019 general election campaign.

Ken McCallum giving a speech today.   Extremists holding anti-immigration opinions are becoming increasingly likely to consider carrying out terrorist attacks against immigration centres and asylum hotels in the UK, Ken McCallum, the head of MI5, has warned.

Ken McCallum has said that Moscow did attempt to interfere in the 2016 Brexit referendum with anti-EU coverage on RT and Sputnik media and via troll social media accounts. But there was a big difference between “what may have been attempted and what actually resulted”, he added. (See 1.15pm.)

Nigel Farage has denied that a Reform UK government would authorise lethal force against small boat crossings in the Channel, hours after one of his MPs said the Royal Marines should be permitted to fire on the boats.

John Healey should “stay the course” and continue repairing the UK’s public finances, the International Monetary Fund’s top economist has said, after the fund lifted its growth forecast for Britain.

Photograph: Will Colebourne/PAShare1h ago17.14 BSTStreeting says, if Sinn Féin opposing new Troubles bill as 'veterans' charter', he's 'delighted'Wes Streeting, the defence secretary, is still giving evidence to the defence committee. Asked about the Northern Ireland Troubles bill, he said that the new amendments being tabled (see 2.34pm) considerably improved it from the point of view of the armed forces. He went on:

double quotation markAnd so we are in a much stronger place, to the extent that I think Sinn Féin have condemned these amendments and the bill as a veterans’ charter, which as far as I’m concerned is the highest plaudit possible, and I’m absolutely delighted that that’s where we’ve got to.

We have worked intensively with the Northern Ireland secretary [Chris Bryant] and his team to get this bill to a much better place, that deals with what I think is my personal moral obligation to people who’ve served.

2h ago16.58 BSTEd Davey under pressure to defend his leadership at meeting with his MPsLiberal Democrat MPs are holding a private meeting later where they are expected to thrash out disagreements about Ed Davey’s leadership. For months there has been persistent, low-level grumbling about Davey’s supposedly ineffectual leadership. This is a long way off the sort of firing squad revolt the Tory 1922 Committee used to specialise in. So far only two relatively junior frontbenchers have resigned.

But it must be a bit serious because at the Times they have activated a loyalty spreadsheet. This is from Aubrey Allegretti on the state of play.

double quotation markLib Dem leadership showdown:

- 4-hours has been carved out in MPs’ diaries for their meeting at 5pm today, to accommodate requests from more than 40 people to speak (and breaks in proceedings for votes). Roz Savage, as chair of the parliamentary party, will chair the meeting.

- So far, I’ve counted 21 MPs who’ve explicitly - or at least appeared - to back Ed Davey. That leaves a *lot* still undeclared. The rebels need 18 (or 25% of MPs) to force a no-confidence vote.

- Davey’s critics are digging in - and hoping his performance tonight swings sceptics in their favour. They say even if he survives tonight, it’s a matter of “when, not if” he goes.

- Davey’s allies accuse the rebels of “trying to create chaos at a pivotal moment, with the timing of the next general election up in the air”. He has spoken to some MPs to encourage them to speak in support of him tonight.

- Some MPs privately think Davey should go, but are divided over who should replace him - further splintering the rebels.

But my colleague Peter Walker reckons Davey is safe for now.

double quotation markFrom what I hear there is almost no chance of Ed Davey facing any kind of no confidence vote at tonight’s meeting of the Lib Dem parliamentary party. Some MPs are dissatisfied with him, even if it’s hard to gauge how many. But there seems a willingness to listen to what he has to say

double quotation markTwo other reasons why anything dramatic feels unlikely:

• There is no consensus among the malcontents - or anyone else – about who they might want to replace Davey.

• The Lib Dems aren’t generally very good at this sort of thing.

2h ago16.38 BSTStreeting tells MPs committing to spending 3% of GDP on defence without plan to fund it would risk Truss-type backlashThe government could trigger a Liz Truss mini-budget-type economic incident if it committed to spend 3% of GDP on defence by 2030 without saying where the money will come from, Wes Streeting has suggested.

Streeting used the argument as he gave evidence to the Commons defence committee, where he as pressed to confirm that the government will raise defence spending to 3% of GDP by 2030.

The defence investment plan (Dip) currently sets out a path to spending 2.7% of GDP on defence by the 2027-28 financial year. John Healey resigned as defence secretary when Keir Starmer refused to commit to 3% by 2030. Healey is now chancellor, but he has not yet explained how he will raise defence spending to the 3% level he treated as a resignation issue.

Streeting told the committee he never expected Healey to set out a pathway to 3% at the budget later this month and that plan was always due in the spending review, now reportedly expected next autumn.

And he defended the chancellor’s decision not to rush. He said:

double quotation markWe have had very bitter recent experience of a former prime minister making unfunded commitments to spend more, tax less, and borrow more all simultaneously, and it led to enormous loss of confidence, people’s mortgages going up, and a level of fundamental loss of confidence in Britain among investors, and this country is still recovering from that.

But Streeting also said that he was “confident that we will get there”, arguing that this confidence was justified “from the choices that Labour’s already made in government through to how strongly, as a matter of principle, the chancellor felt about this”.

View image in fullscreenWes Streeting at the Commons defence committee. Photograph: House of Commons/UK Parliament/PAShareUpdated at 17.23 BST3h ago15.36 BSTPat McFadden accuses Tories of hypocrisy over pensions triple lock, saying many of them accept current version unsustainablePat McFadden, the work and pensions secretary, has claimed he has a file “as thick as my morning porridge” with quotes from Tories arguing against the pensions triple lock.

He made the claim in a Commons statement explaining the plan announced by Andy Burnham at Labour conference to replace the current triple lock with an adjusted version that will be less generous.

The Conservatives opposed the move when it was announced and, in the Commons, McFadden’s Tory shadow, Helen Whately, claimed this policy was a “U-turn in waiting” and that it would be abandoned by Burnham because of its unpopularity.
